summary: Gives guidelines so protocols can move from one mandatory-to-implement cryptographic algorithm suite to another over time. It discusses algorithm agility and how to choose the algorithms that every implementation must support.

eli5.summary: Locks get old, so this explains how to design things so you can swap in better locks later.

questions: what does should+ mean in an rfc
why are weak algorithms hard to remove
subtitle: How to design protocols so that aging cryptography can be swapped out, and how to pick the algorithms every implementation must support.

tldr.problem: Cryptographic algorithms weaken with time, but peers must share a common set of algorithms, and weak ones tend to linger long after experts say to move on.
tldr.mechanism: Protocols should identify the algorithm or suite in use, specify strong mandatory-to-implement algorithms in a companion document, protect the negotiation from downgrade, and keep the set of choices small.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Best Current Practice (BCP 201) giving guidance to IETF working groups and protocol authors; it defines no wire protocol and creates no IANA registries.

facts.label: SHA-1 to SHA-256 transition
facts.value: More than five years to widespread use

today: RFC 7696 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 201) and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the IETF's guidance on algorithm agility.

sections.title: Why Algorithms Need to Be Replaceable
sections.content:
Many IETF protocols use cryptography for confidentiality, integrity, authentication or digital signatures. For interoperability, peers must support a common set of algorithms, often called a cipher suite.

Algorithms age. As cryptanalysis improves and computing power grows, breaking an algorithm gets cheaper. The RFC tells designers to assume that any algorithm will eventually become obsolete, so protocols need ways to migrate from one suite to another. This ability is algorithm agility.

An identifier alone is not enough. People who maintain implementations and run services must also deploy and configure the new algorithms and disable the old ones. Experience has shown this is hard, mostly because of interoperability worries, so weak algorithms often stay in use long after experts recommend migration.
sections.eli5: Everything wears out eventually, even secret codes. If you plan ahead for swapping the code, you are not stuck when it breaks.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifiers and Registries
sections.content:
Protocols that use cryptography MUST support one or more algorithms or suites, and MUST include a way to say which one is in use. The identifier can be carried in the protocol or established by management, for example a key table entry that holds a key and an algorithm identifier.

Without an identifier, a protocol version number or another major change is needed to move to a new algorithm. Including an identifier is described as a minimal step toward agility.

Designs can carry one identifier per algorithm or one per full suite, and designers should pick one approach and use it consistently. Suite identifiers keep selections complete and compatible but face a combinatoric explosion as algorithms are added. Per-algorithm identifiers force implementations to decide at run time which combinations are acceptable. The RFC calls both IKEv2 (separate identifiers) and TLS (suite identifiers) fine design choices.

An IANA registry SHOULD be used for these identifiers. Entries should not be changed or removed once added, but they should be markable as deprecated.
sections.eli5: Put a name tag on every lock so everyone knows which one is on the door. Then you can say "we use the new lock now" and everybody understands.

sections.title: Mandatory-to-Implement Algorithms
sections.content:
Following RFC 3365, IETF protocols that use cryptography MUST specify one or more strong mandatory-to-implement algorithms or suites. This does not force every deployment to use them, only to make them available everywhere.

The IETF needs to change that set over time without rewriting the base protocol, so the RFC RECOMMENDs that the base specification refer to a companion algorithms document. The set SHOULD be kept small and the transition SHOULD happen before the current algorithms weaken to the breaking point.

Where a protocol is embedded in another, the system-level specification picks the algorithms. For example, S/MIME chooses them rather than CMS. The algorithm specification MUST identify the key sizes and parameter sizes to support, and the mandatory key size is expected to grow over time.

To warn implementers about coming changes, authors SHOULD give notice. One approach, first used in RFC 4307, adds three terms:

  • SHOULD+: like SHOULD, but likely to become a MUST.
  • SHOULD-: like SHOULD, but likely to be deprecated to a MAY or worse.
  • MUST-: like MUST, but expected to be downgraded, probably to at least a SHOULD or SHOULD-.
sections.eli5: Everyone agrees on one strong lock that every door must be able to use. A note on the door says which lock is about to be replaced.

sections.title: Transitioning Away from Weak Algorithms
sections.content:
Specifying a better algorithm is easy. Moving everyone to it is not, because knowledge of the new algorithm's deployment is always imperfect. Transition works best as part of algorithm selection or negotiation, where peers pick the best option both support and their policies allow. A way to learn whether the new algorithm is actually deployed is also needed. The RFC points to SMIMECapabilities in S/MIME and the DNSSEC EDNS0 option as examples, and to RFC 6916 for RPKI, where a second signature algorithm is introduced and the original is phased out.

In the worst case an algorithm is flawed enough that a casual attacker can break it with a simple script. Then one may want to reject the weak suite well before the new one is widely deployed. In any case a time comes to refuse the old algorithm, on a flag day or on dates each installation chooses.

Deprecation is hard because people do not like to cause interoperability problems, even for security. Implementers hesitate to remove deprecated algorithms and administrators hesitate to disable them. Browser visual warnings for deprecated algorithms are cited as a new incentive. Long-lived intermediate CA certificates make infrastructure transition especially slow, and organizations with significant influence can help by coordinating the end of a suite.
sections.eli5: Switching to a better lock is the easy part. Getting every family to actually swap theirs, and to stop using the old one, takes a long time.

sections.title: Protecting Negotiation and Balancing Strength
sections.content:
Algorithm selection or negotiation SHOULD be integrity protected. Otherwise the protocol is open to a downgrade attack, and the attempt to transition may create new openings. Designers must also consider which algorithm protects the negotiation itself: a flaw in a single mandatory-to-implement integrity algorithm could let an attacker influence the choice of all the others.

Key establishment needs care too. Frameworks such as EAP and SASL make the key establishment approach itself negotiable, so that negotiation must be protected before it is used to produce keys. If authentication of the negotiation fails, the only recourse is to start over.

The algorithms in a suite SHOULD be roughly equal in strength, and designers SHOULD give clear guidance so deployers get balanced options. Wrapping one key with a key of a different size yields the strength of the shorter key. For example, a 128-bit AES content key wrapped by a 256-bit AES key gives at most 128 bits of protection. Any aspect of the algorithm not named by the identifier, including key size and parameters, needs to be negotiated.

Complex negotiation and support for many alternatives both create rarely used code with undiscovered bugs, so implementations should stay as simple as possible. Opportunistic security (RFC 7435) may accept weaker algorithms when no strong ones are shared, as long as this does not facilitate downgrade attacks, though strong algorithms are always preferable.
sections.eli5: When two kids pick a secret code, nobody should be able to sneak in and trick them into choosing the weakest one. And a strong chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

sections.title: Choosing Algorithms and the Cost of Choice
sections.content:
Ideally two independent sets of mandatory-to-implement algorithms are specified, a primary and a secondary suite, so the secondary is already widely deployed if the primary breaks. Fallback algorithms must be diverse and routinely exercised, which is hard when they need different credentials.

Mandatory-to-implement algorithms MUST have a stable public specification and well-studied public documentation. The IETF prefers unencumbered algorithms, widely deployed ones, and ones resistant to side-channel attacks that fit a wide range of performance, power and code size limits. Reusing the same algorithms across protocols simplifies implementation. Sometimes two are justified: AES-CCM is available in hardware in many small devices, while AES-GCM is parallelizable and suited to high-speed devices.

Too many choices are harmful, since weak ciphers stick around once deployed. Picking one true suite is harmful too. WEP was the only encryption in the first IEEE 802.11 specification and its replacement took very large effort. The SHA-1 to SHA-256 transition took more than five years from specification to widespread use. Even the simplest protocol needs a version number to signal the algorithm.

National cipher suites, mandated by law or regulation, may lack wide public review. The default server or responder configuration SHOULD disable them so an administrator must enable them where required.
sections.eli5: Having a hundred kinds of locks is a mess, but having only one kind is risky if it breaks. The trick is a small, well-chosen set, with a spare.

sections.title: Security Considerations and IANA
sections.content:
Security improves when weak algorithms can be replaced easily. Keeping algorithms separate from parsing code and state machines also makes it easier to handle concerns such as key exposure and constant-time execution.

Sometimes the algorithm is fine but its use in the protocol is attacked. TLS originally did MAC-then-encrypt, which is no longer considered secure, so RFC 7366 specified encrypt-then-MAC. Such cases may need protocol changes, not just new algorithms. Protocols that protect stored data, such as S/MIME, must keep supporting old algorithms to recover old data.

Hardware is a challenge: many tiny devices cannot update firmware at all, and high-end data center equipment may need board-level replacement. Certification of health or safety devices and long upgrade cycles in embedded and SCADA systems slow things further. Because replacement takes so long, the transition needs to start when practically exploitable flaws become known.

Measurements SHOULD be used to see whether implemented algorithms are actually used, and unused ones SHOULD be marked deprecated in the IANA registry. In short, eliminate the cruft. The RFC creates no new registries and adds no entries, but recommends the convention that registered identifiers are not changed or removed.
sections.eli5: Some gadgets cannot be updated at all, so they are stuck with the old lock. That is why planning early and cleaning out unused locks both matter.
